zh-CN.Use explicit geometric counterexamples t: Use explicit geometric counterexamples to separate an area lower bound, a feasible cutting layout, and a proof of optimality under stated constraints.
zh-CN.An estimate based on total part area ans: An estimate based on total part area answers a different question from a layout containing every required rectangle. Serairi and Haouari's 2018 paper [1] studies lower bounds for fixed-orientation two-dimensional bin packing. SCIP's bin-packing documentation [2] provides a simpler capacity-model reference. This article derives its own small geometric examples to explain the distinction for sheet cutting. It does not reproduce the paper's benchmark or claim that WoodCutTool implements its bounds. Every example states its dimensions and omitted constraints, so a mathematical conclusion cannot silently become a physical cutting guarantee.
zh-CN.If all sheets have usable area A and req: If all sheets have usable area A and required parts have total area S, any complete layout needs at least ceil(S/A) sheets. The argument is conservation of area: N sheets cannot hold more than NA of non-overlapping parts. Use usable dimensions after defined edge exclusions and keep different material groups separate. The bound ignores how rectangles occupy the space, their orientation, cut access, and the area removed by actual kerf paths. It is therefore necessary, but generally insufficient. It can reject an impossibly low count without constructing a feasible plan at that count.
zh-CN.Take a 1000 × 1000 mm sheet and two requ: Take a 1000 × 1000 mm sheet and two required 600 × 600 mm squares. Their combined area is 720,000 mm², so the area bound is one sheet. Yet the two squares cannot fit as axis-aligned, non-overlapping rectangles on one sheet. To avoid overlap, their projections must be disjoint on at least one axis. Either separation would require 600 + 600 = 1200 mm, exceeding that sheet dimension. Rotation by 90 degrees changes nothing because the items are squares. Two sheets are feasible, so this small instance has an optimum of two despite its one-sheet area bound.
zh-CN.Kerf Changes the Feasibility Question Ag: Kerf Changes the Feasibility Question Again
zh-CN.Now take four 500 × 500 mm squares. With: Now take four 500 × 500 mm squares. With a zero-kerf geometric model and no trim, they tile the same sheet exactly. With a positive 3 mm cutting kerf, a physical plan cannot obtain all four exact squares from that sheet: the parts already consume all its area before any material is removed. Four 498.5 × 498.5 mm squares instead satisfy 2 × 498.5 + 3 = 1000 in each direction and admit an ideal two-by-two guillotine cutting plan without trim. That latter construction still assumes exact stock, exact kerf, usable edges, and appropriate cutting access.
zh-CN.A verified plan using three sheets suppl: A verified plan using three sheets supplies an upper bound of three for the modeled problem: the optimum can be no worse than that known feasible result. An area lower bound of two does not prove a better two-sheet plan exists. It leaves an unresolved gap. If a complete, constraint-valid two-sheet plan is found and a valid lower bound is also two, the modeled optimum is established. A failed heuristic attempt at one sheet is not a general infeasibility proof. Be explicit about which bounds are justified and whether the solver result is complete.
zh-CN.Verify a Layout as a Certificate: Verify a Layout as a Certificate
zh-CN.For an inspectable layout, preserve each: For an inspectable layout, preserve each part's identifier, quantity instance, material, sheet assignment, coordinates, and orientation. Check all required instances are present exactly once, all placements remain within usable stock, and no prohibited overlap occurs. Then check the specific kerf model, trim exclusions, grain restrictions, defects, and cut sequence used by the workflow. A pixel preview alone can conceal a missing quantity or a coordinate error. Conversely, coordinate validity in a zero-kerf packing model does not establish that a particular saw can execute the sequence. Keep those certificates distinct.
zh-CN.A Reproducible Benchmark Needs More Than: A Reproducible Benchmark Needs More Than a Screenshot
zh-CN.A proposed solver comparison would freez: A proposed solver comparison would freeze the input data, allowed rotations, material groups, kerf convention, and termination budget before running either method. Publish rejected or incomplete cases alongside successful ones. Record the solver version and deterministic seed where applicable. Retain the actual placements rather than only the final sheet count, so feasibility can be checked independently. If one method has additional cut-access constraints, compare that constrained problem explicitly. A lower count from a looser model is not evidence that the stricter workflow wastes material unnecessarily.
zh-CN.For the first constructed instance, the: For the first constructed instance, the projection argument and the two-sheet construction prove the optimum under the specified axis-aligned model. For a real cut list, the strength of the conclusion depends on validated inputs, feasible placements, and appropriate bounds. An area estimate remains useful for an early purchasing screen, provided its status stays visible. A shop-ready release also needs stock inspection and an executable cutting review. The paired-benchmark article linked below addresses how to compare planning methods without allowing differences between projects to masquerade as improvements in the algorithm.
Label the area total as a lower bound.

zh-CN.Claim optimality only with matching vali: Claim optimality only with matching valid bounds or another proof.
